title_original: Andrew Nadolski Lays the Forest Bare

blocks.text: British photographer Andrew Nadolski devoted more than a decade to less than one square mile of wooded valley on the edge of Dartmoor. The resulting book, The White Wood , leads us into this leafless wood as if into the kingdom of shadows.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Andrew Nadolski .

blocks.caption: From The White Wood 2026 © Andrew Nadolski

blocks.text: Born in 1964 in Derby, a city in the English Midlands, Andrew Nadolski got his first serious camera, a Pentax ME Super, at eighteen. The young man went off to study graphic design at the art college in Exeter, the county seat of Devon, in the country’s southwest. Preferring the vinegar tang of the darkroom to typography, he took photography classes with Jem Southam, a future master of British landscape. After graduating in 1986, he made his living as a designer and commercial photographer until 2024. His previous book, The End of the Land , devoted to a remote beach in Cornwall, came out in 2005.

blocks.text: In 2013, his former teacher Jem Southam confessed in On Landscape magazine: “I have tried Dartmoor but it is a particularly challenging place to make pictures.” The student nonetheless clings to the rim of that granite upland, where the River Dart carves a deep gorge, and the master, now his publisher, calls his pictures “exquisite.” “To descend into it is to cross a threshold and enter a far older landscape,” says Andrew Nadolski. Only in winter does he shoot this remnant of temperate rainforest, sodden with moss and lichen, when the fall of the leaves shows off the trees’ bare bones.

blocks.text: His long exposures turn rapids to milk, blur the wind-whipped branches and keep the moss-gloved trunks crisp. An ash gray washes over these views, printed in three inks. Mist thickens the picture as much as the silence: “sound is absorbed and distance becomes uncertain,” writes the photographer, gripped by “a sense of foreboding.” The path leads down toward Luckey Tor, a granite outcrop almost entirely hidden by vegetation, which the author likens to “the remnant of some ancient ruin.” Shivers. Local legend has it that the Dart demands a sacrifice: “River Dart, every year thou claim’st a heart.”
